query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An active learning–based machine‐learning workflow that combines short, strategically sampled ab initio simulations with covariance‐based vibrational entropy extraction and Gaussian process–assisted thermodynamic integration can reproduce the free energies of both solid and fluid phases—with their vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions—at a fraction of the cost of full AIMD and TOR-TILD, even for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental to multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting temperature (i.e. solid and corresponding high-temperature fluid states).
generation.intervention: Deploy a two-stage computational scheme: first, use an active learning protocol to train an ML potential (e.g., deep potential or moment tensor potential) from short ab initio MD trajectories that sample key configurations; second, apply a free-energy integration method that combines covariance-based vibrational entropy extraction (capturing anharmonicity) with Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to efficiently integrate free energy gradients across the phase transition.
generation.conditions: Tested in the high-temperature regime (e.g., 0.8–1.2 times the experimental melting temperature) for multicomponent high-entropy alloys and analogous elemental/binary systems where conventional AIMD/TOR-TILD protocols are currently used.
generation.structural_mediator: The covariance matrix of atomic displacements—used to extract effective vibrational density of states and entropy—which mediates the inclusion of anharmonic effects and indirectly accounts for electron–vibration coupling via evaluations at temperature‐appropriate lattice parameters.
generation.mechanism: The ML potential reproduces the essential free-energy landscape with high fidelity using far fewer ab initio data points; coupled with a fast, covariance-based assessment of vibrational entropy and a GPR‐enhanced integration of free energy gradients, the approach approximates the full free-energy difference between phases (including anharmonic and electron–vibration effects) with significant computational savings.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion free-energy curves and melting (fusion) temperatures predicted by the ML-enhanced workflow will agree with those from explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD within an acceptable error (e.g., <10% deviation) while reducing computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics calculations (with full vibrational, anharmonic, and electron coupling included) and the TOR-TILD method as applied to elemental and binary systems.
generation.boundary: The method should work for systems where atomic displacements remain moderate so that the Gaussian (covariance) approximation is valid (e.g., crystalline solids and disordered fluids near melting); it may be less accurate for molecular solids with large-amplitude bond rotations or for systems with extreme electronic structure changes that challenge ML potential transferability.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from covariance-based entropy extraction (PMC9141984::web::000::abstract) and ML-assisted free energy evaluations in catalysis (PMC10569033::web::000::abstract, PMC7704029::web::001::introduction) supports rapid yet accurate free-energy estimation, the approach’s transferability to complex high-entropy systems and its ability to capture subtle electron–vibration couplings remain to be demonstrated in this new context.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a multicomponent high-entropy alloy system near its melting temperature and compute the free-energy difference between the solid and fluid phases using (a) the new ML-enhanced workflow and (b) full AIMD/TOR-TILD calculations. Vary the training set density and temperature sampling to test robustness.
measurements: Absolute free energies for solid and fluid phases
Fusion (melting) temperature determined from the free-energy crossover
Quantification of vibrational and anharmonic entropy contributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-enhanced workflow yields free-energy differences or predicted fusion temperatures that deviate by more than 10% from those obtained by the explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD method, or if the extracted vibrational/anharmonic contributions fail to match independent estimates, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Predicting the rate constants of elementary reaction steps is key for the computational modeling of catalytic processes. Within transition state theory (TST), this requires an accurate estimation of the corresponding free energy barriers. While sophisticated methods for estimating free energy differences exist, these typically require extensive (biased) molecular dynamics simulations that are computationally prohibitive with the first-principles electronic structure methods that are typically used in catalysis research. In this contribution, we show that machine-learning (ML) interatomic potentials can be trained in an automated iterative workflow to perform such free energy calculations at a much reduced computational cost as compared to a direct density functional theory (DFT) based evaluation. For the decomposition of CHO on Rh(111), we find that thermal effects are substantial and lead to a decrease in the free energy barrier, which can be vanishingly small, depending on the DFT functional used. Machine learning techniques are increasingly used to bypass expensive quantum chemical computations. Typical examples are machine learning-based potentials that are exploited to propagate the dynamical evolution of molecular systems on ab initio potentials at a fraction of the cost. The seminal work in the field comes from Behler and Parrinello, who trained a generalized Artificial Neural Network (ANN) capable of predicting density functional theory-based energies and atomic forces and demonstrated its capability on bulk silicon and then on carbon, and sodium. Behler and Marquetand then applied the same approach to n-alkanes and alanine tripeptides. Comparable capabilities were achieved by Csanyi and co-workers, who used kernel-based method (i.e., the Gaussian approximation potential) to propagate the density functional theory (DFT)–molecular dynamics (MD) of bulk crystal, amorphous carbon, and silicon. Kernel ridge methods were also exploited for the “on-the-fly” propagation of the dynamic in the electronic states, circumventing the need for the explicit time dependent DFT or the CASSCF computations. AbstractThe vibrational entropy of a solid at finite temperature is investigated from the perspective of information theory. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations generate ensembles of atomic configurations at finite temperature from which we obtain the N-body distribution of atomic displacements, ρN. We calculate the information-theoretic entropy from the expectation value of lnρN. At a first level of approximation, treating individual atomic displacements independently, our method may be applied using Debye–Waller B-factors, allowing diffraction experiments to obtain an upper bound on the thermodynamic entropy. At the next level of approximation we correct the overestimation through inclusion of displacement covariances. We apply this approach to elemental body-centered cubic sodium and face-centered cubic aluminum, showing good agreement with experimental values above the Debye temperatures of the metals. Below the Debye temperatures, we extract an effective vibrational density of states from eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, and then evaluate the entropy quantum mechanically, again yielding good agreement with experiment down to low temperatures.
